title: Props, the kazoo mute and the kazoo craze
summary: He used props like a tin barrel and derbies, and invented a kazoo mute for his horn that others copied.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: And so we used to open up this thing and I used to wave that hat, you know, and people kept saying, what's going on? Some lady in Boston interviewed me one time. I think she was with the Boston Travelers, a musical critic. And she came backstage, we were playing in Boston. And I used to have carried tin cans and derbies and a little barrel with a skin head on it. You got used for a tom-tom.

And I picked that up and it got painted all the gild and diamonds all over it. I'd stand up in it with a spotlight on me and I'd wave that little barrel out to them. So this lady come, she come one morning, she come over and of course she called the hotel and asked me to go for an interview. I said, yeah. So she, all these different props that you use, what are they? I said, I explained, she couldn't get into her head what it were. And you actually get music out of them? And I said, hey, that's something. Yeah. Yeah. Can I see them? I said, we're over the theater. Well, when are you going over the theater? Oh, I go, everybody. If you want to go, take a walk home. So we were looking at the Copa Pass in Boston. Walked over to the Keith's Theater and went backstage. And, oh, she was amazed. She was really astounded. And the funny thing about the, you hear about these kazoos, you know, these guys. Well, I bought my little, yeah, I bought my kid a kazoo, you know. He, I'd sit down and he'd run over the horn once in a while, you know, and the kid would sit down and he wanted to, wanted to play, he was singing through a piece of paper, see. So I went downtown when they asked for us a kazoo, I got him a kazoo. And he can play a kazoo.
Do it, do it, do it, do it.

So while we're playing, I'm playing, and so finally he takes his kazoo and he sticks it in the horn. While I'm playing, I said, now wait, don't do that, no. He was a little chap about two years old. He got a dang thing in the, he said, hey, here's the sound. So I went and got a couple of corks and I got some sealing wax and I sealed these two corks on the side. Yeah. And stuck it in the horn.
I've seen where they sell, they sold them like that for a while.

Yeah, that's me though. Everybody around Chicago's got kazoos. They all copied that from yours. Yeah, then the Trombones put three kazoos together, see. Yeah. They fit in the big bell. And son of a gun, I don't copyright it, I just let it go. You should have patented it, yeah.
And you made a little money out of it maybe.

Sure, well, I, so that, that, that was a kazoo craze, you know. Yeah. But, well, you know, you, being, I was a young fellow, I hadn't had any idea about doing it all that, you know. Well, we're just about out of this tape.
